source.title: Transcoders Trace Visual Grounding and Hallucinations in Vision-Language Models
source.authors: Dimitrios Damianos; Leon Voukoutis; G. Skyrianos; Vassilis Katsouros; Georgios Paraskevopoulos

record.tranche_reason: Applies sparse feature decomposition to a generative vision-language model and measures properties of its extracted features, providing evidence relevant to feature distribution in a real model.
record.gate_note: The study reports feature-sharing and feature-count measurements in Appendix B.5. Patch-ablation comparisons, false-visual-grounding results, circuit-tracing visualizations, and hallucination-classification results are not rows because they do not measure the feature-distribution claims in the versions.
record.test_reason: The study uses transcoders and SAEs on Gemma 3-4B-IT as tools for visual-grounding attribution and hallucination analysis, and mainly reports its own method's performance. Its one side analysis (Appendix B.5) counts how many distinct tokens each transcoder feature fires on. That measure is token-level feature reuse in a dictionary, not neuron-level spread, SAE recovery of sparse features (V4), or completeness, stability or canonicality of dictionary features (V5). A feature firing on many tokens can still encode one concept, so it does not cleanly measure polysemanticity either. It is recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but it is a minor appendix point. The authors' main conclusions are that transcoder attributions beat SAE attributions for visual grounding under patch ablation. They also conclude that the pathways are specific to vision-language interaction (FVG ablations give ∆p≈0), and that circuit-graph structure predicts hallucination at AUC 0.68. In B.5 they state that extracted features are not monosemantic and that the model uses a distributed scheme, with rare tokens activating about 40% more features.
record.recipe_differences: This study measures sparse transcoder feature sharing in a trained VLM; it does not test the toy-network superposition setup. It also compares SAE and transcoder attributions for visual grounding.

fits_no_version.finding: In Gemma 3-4B-IT transcoders (top-64, 40,960 features per layer), on 10k Flickr30K samples, only 4 features (0.01%) fire for a single token. 51.4% fire for 21–100 tokens and 45 fire for every token. Rare tokens activate more features per layer (49.4) than frequent tokens (35.4).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Transcoder/dictionary features in a VLM are broadly shared across tokens rather than token-specific; the number of active features rises for rarer tokens.

record.problems: The feature-sharing analysis is on one model and 10,000 Flickr30K samples. The study itself notes that it focuses on Gemma 3-4B-IT and that its analyses use relatively small sample sizes. Its feature-sharing analysis does not establish neuron-level spread or SAE feature recovery.
record.rows_left_out: No additional claim-relevant results were reported beyond the Appendix B.5 feature-sharing table and token-frequency comparison.

untested.parts: All: no toy models, sparsity transitions or geometry.
All: no test of capacity pressure or dedicated vs shared dimensions.
All: no analysis of non-capacity causes of polysemantic neurons.
No neuron-level spread measured. Dictionary reconstruction (FVU ≈0.05) is reported only as method selection, not as a test of sparse feature recovery.
Completeness, stability and canonicality of dictionary features are not tested.

record.verdict_notes: The record's V4 'supports' label is removed. The B.5 measure is token-sharing of transcoder features, which the authors call monosemanticity, but it does not match any version's construct. Top-k=64 sparsity bounds the active-feature counts, which confounds the rare/frequent comparison. Table 1 FVU values (transcoder top-64 0.049, SAE 0.048) are method-selection numbers and rightly not rows. One model, small samples, preprint.

versions.untested_parts: Toy networks with more sparse features than dimensions, their geometry, and sparsity-dependent transitions.
Whether capacity pressure explains polysemanticity or whether important features receive dedicated dimensions.
Whether polysemantic neurons arise for reasons other than capacity pressure.
The study measures sharing among transcoder features across tokens in one VLM; it does not measure features spread across neurons or directly test SAE feature recovery.
SAE feature completeness, stability, or canonicality.
Whether underlying features are one-dimensional directions or multidimensional.

rows.subject: Gemma 3-4B-IT
rows.operation_detail: Measured how many distinct tokens shared each active feature.
rows.measure: Distribution of active features by number of tokens sharing them
rows.note: The paper says these results indicate a distributed representational scheme rather than one-to-one mapping between features and concepts. The measurement concerns transcoder features, not neuron-level feature distribution or SAE recovery.
rows.check: Counts distinct tokens per transcoder feature (Table 5). It does not measure features spread across neurons or whether a dictionary recovers sparse features. No baseline exists for expected token-sharing under a monosemantic dictionary. Token-level sharing is not the same as semantic polysemanticity, so V4 cannot be read from it.

rows.subject: Gemma 3-4B-IT
rows.operation_detail: Measured the average number of features activated per layer for rare tokens.
rows.measure: Average number of features activated per layer
rows.note: The paper compares this with high-frequency tokens and describes an inverse relationship between token frequency and number of activated features.
rows.check: Average active features per layer for rare tokens (49.4). The transcoders use top-64 sparsity, so active-feature counts are capped by construction. The number bears on no version's effect.

rows.subject: Gemma 3-4B-IT
rows.operation_detail: Measured the average number of features activated per layer for high-frequency tokens.
rows.measure: Average number of features activated per layer
rows.note: The paper reports this alongside 49.4 for rare tokens and describes the difference as an approximately 40% increase for rare tokens.
rows.check: Average active features for high-frequency tokens (35.4); the frequency threshold is not stated. Same top-k construction caveat as B5-rare. It does not measure any version's effect.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Gemma 3-4B-IT transcoder features in the Flickr30K analysis
reader_labels.reason: Most measured features are shared across multiple tokens, which supports feature sharing rather than one-to-one feature-to-concept mapping (B5-sharing; the frequency comparison is in B5-rare and B5-high-frequency).
